summary:
Two metadata-carrying formats dominate sprite-sheet interchange, and both share the same frame geometry vocabulary. The Aseprite export JSON (written by `aseprite --sheet out.png --data out.json --format json-hash|json-array`) stores per frame: "frame" {x,y,w,h} (rect on the sheet), "rotated", "trimmed", "spriteSourceSize" {x,y,w,h} (trim offset inside the untrimmed canvas), "sourceSize" {w,h}, and "duration" in milliseconds — verified against a real export (labs.phaser.io paladin.json). Its "meta" block adds "frameTags" [{name, from, to, direction}] with direction "forward" | "reverse" | "pingpong" | "pingpong_reverse" (plus a "repeat" count in Aseprite 1.3+), optional "layers" and "slices" (slices carry bounds, 9-patch center, and pivot). TexturePacker's generic "JSON (hash)" / "JSON (array)" formats use the identical frame fields but replace "duration" with an optional normalized "pivot" {x,y}; its Phaser 3 exporter instead writes "anchor" and wraps everything in a "textures" array (one entry per multipack page, each with its own image/size/scale). PixiJS consumes the same hash format plus an "animations" block ({"walk": ["walk01.png", ...]}) that feeds AnimatedSprite directly; meta.scale maps to resolution and meta.related_multi_packs/linkedSheets handle multipack. The native binary .aseprite format (128-byte header, magic 0xA5E0; chunk types Layer 0x2004, Cel 0x2005 zlib-compressed, Tags 0x2018, Palette 0x2019, User Data 0x2020, Slice 0x2022) is moderately complex but is worth considering as a later feature because Unity's official com.unity.2d.aseprite package imports .aseprite files directly into sliced sprites + Animation Clips with per-frame timings, and Aseprite itself becomes a round-trip editor for ImageAI output.

Engine expectations split into three camps. JSON-atlas engines: Phaser 3 (`load.atlas` auto-detects hash vs array; `load.aseprite` + `anims.createFromAseprite` builds animations straight from Aseprite JSON frameTags and durations) and PixiJS (hash + animations block). Editor-slicing engines: Unity (Sprite Mode = Multiple; Sprite Editor slices via Automatic, Grid By Cell Size, or Grid By Cell Count; per-sprite name/rect/pivot/border) and Godot 4, which has no native JSON atlas import — you either grid-slice in the SpriteFrames editor ("Add frames from a Sprite Sheet"), use Sprite2D hframes/vframes/frame with AnimationPlayer, or install the TexturePacker .tpsheet plugin that generates AtlasTexture .tres files. Godot's SpriteFrames stores named animations with per-animation FPS + loop and per-frame relative duration multipliers (duration 2.0 shows twice as long), so millisecond durations must be converted (pick FPS, express frames as multiples). Text-format engines: libGDX's .atlas lists per region xy/size/orig/offset/rotate/index (name_N suffixes become index; findRegions(name) returns ordered animation frames). Unreal Paper2D imports a .paper2dsprites JSON (TexturePacker's UE exporter) and auto-creates sprites + a Flipbook. Conclusion for broadest compatibility: export (a) a plain uniform-grid PNG (universal fallback — Unity, Godot, RPG Maker, and every engine can slice a grid), (b) TexturePacker-style JSON hash with pivot, and (c) Aseprite-style JSON — those three cover essentially every engine and tool.

Grid conventions worth shipping as presets: RPG Maker MV/MZ character sheets are 4 rows (down, left, right, up) × 3 columns (middle column = idle, outer columns = step frames), default 48x48 cells; a full sheet holds 8 characters in a 4×2 arrangement (576×384), and the engine infers cell size as width/12 × height/8 — a "$" filename prefix marks a single-character sheet (144×192, width/3 × height/4) and "!" marks objects that skip the 6 px vertical lift. The LPC "universal spritesheet" uses 64×64 frames on an 832×1344 canvas (13 cols × 21 rows): spellcast 7f, thrust 8f, walk 9f (column 0 = idle stance), slash 6f, shoot 13f — each in 4 direction rows ordered up, left, down, right — plus one 6-frame hurt/die row; LPC art is dual-licensed GPL 3.0 + CC-BY-SA 3.0 (attribution obligations if shipped). For animated single-file exports: GIF (256 colors/frame, 1-bit transparency, delay in 1/100 s — browsers clamp delays ≤10 ms to 100 ms, so 20 ms/50 fps is the reliable floor; disposal methods 1=none, 2=restore-background, 3=restore-previous; NETSCAPE2.0 loop extension) is for chat/forum previews only; APNG (acTL/fcTL/fdAT chunks, delay_num/delay_den rational delays, full 8-bit alpha, PNG-fallback first frame, ~96% browser support) is the best lossless preview with real transparency; animated WebP (ANIM loop count + ANMF per-frame 24-bit millisecond duration, per-frame lossy-or-lossless, alpha, 16383px max) is the smallest web-delivery option. A good internal model must track, per frame: sheet rect, rotated flag, trim offset + untrimmed sourceSize, normalized pivot, duration in ms; per tag: name, frame range, direction/loop mode, repeat count; plus optional slices/9-patch and a palette for indexed export — that superset losslessly projects onto every format above.
key_facts: Aseprite JSON frame entry (verified real export): {"frame":{"x","y","w","h"},"rotated":bool,"trimmed":bool,"spriteSourceSize":{"x","y","w","h"},"sourceSize":{"w","h"},"duration":83} — duration is per-frame in milliseconds

Aseprite meta block: app, version, image, format "RGBA8888", size {w,h}, scale "1"; frameTags entries are {"name","from","to","direction"} with direction values forward | reverse | pingpong | pingpong_reverse (Aseprite 1.3 adds a "repeat" count); slices carry bounds, 9-patch center, and pivot

Aseprite CLI: --sheet out.png --data out.json --format json-hash|json-array; --sheet-type horizontal|vertical|rows|columns|packed; --list-tags/--list-slices/--list-layers gate what lands in meta; padding via --border-padding / --shape-padding / --inner-padding; filename-format placeholders {title} {tag} {frame} {tagframe} {duration} {layer}

Native .aseprite format: little-endian, 128-byte header magic 0xA5E0, per-frame header magic 0xF1FA; chunks: Layer 0x2004, Cel 0x2005 (zlib/DEFLATE pixel data), Tags 0x2018 (loop direction bytes 0=forward 1=reverse 2=pingpong 3=pingpong-reverse), Palette 0x2019, User Data 0x2020, Slice 0x2022, Tileset 0x2023; color depths 8bpp indexed / 16bpp grayscale / 32bpp RGBA — a writer is moderate effort (binary structs + zlib), and worth it mainly because Unity consumes the format

Unity's official 2D Aseprite Importer package (com.unity.2d.aseprite, Unity 2022.2+) imports .aseprite/.ase directly: individual frame timings, tags become Animation Clips (repeating per tag setting), layer groups/opacity, generates a read-only Animator Controller

TexturePacker generic JSON hash/array frame fields are identical to Aseprite's geometry fields but with optional normalized "pivot":{"x":0.5,"y":0.5} instead of duration; meta adds smartupdate hash; exporter list includes JSON hash/array, XML, Unity (.tpsheet), Godot (.tpsheet), Phaser, Pixi, cocos2d plist, LibGDX, Unreal Paper2D, Spine, EaselJS, CSS, SpriteKit, MonoGame

TexturePacker Phaser 3 exporter: per-frame "anchor" (not pivot), and a single JSON with a "textures" ARRAY (one entry per multipack page, each with own image/size/scale/frames) — loaded via this.load.multiatlas; it is the only TexturePacker format supporting pivot editing + single-file multipack + normal-map packing

TexturePacker trim modes: None, Trim (keeps sourceSize reference), CropKeepPos, Crop (resets position), Polygon; algorithms MaxRects/Grid/Basic/Polygon; --enable-rotation packs frames rotated 90° (consumer must support "rotated":true — safest default is rotation OFF)

Phaser 3: this.load.atlas(key, png, json) auto-detects JSON hash vs array; this.load.aseprite(key, png, json) + this.anims.createFromAseprite(key) builds animations from Aseprite frameTags with per-frame durations — exporting Aseprite JSON gives Phaser animation import for free

PixiJS Spritesheet JSON: frames hash with frame/spriteSourceSize/sourceSize/anchor per frame, plus "animations":{"enemy":["enemy1.png","enemy2.png"]} consumed by new AnimatedSprite(sheet.animations[name]); meta.scale maps to texture resolution; multipack via linked sheets (meta.related_multi_packs in TexturePacker pixi output)

Godot 4 SpriteFrames resource: named animations, per-animation speed in FPS + loop, per-frame texture + RELATIVE duration multiplier ("a frame with duration 2.0 is displayed twice as long as 1.0") — converting per-frame ms requires choosing an FPS and expressing frames as multiples (GCD of durations works)

Godot 4 has NO native JSON atlas import: options are (a) SpriteFrames editor "Add frames from a Sprite Sheet" grid slicer (set horizontal/vertical counts), (b) Sprite2D properties hframes/vframes/frame + AnimationPlayer, (c) CodeAndWeb's TexturePacker Importer plugin reading .tpsheet into AtlasTexture .tres files — or ImageAI could emit a .tres SpriteFrames/AtlasTexture text resource directly (AtlasTexture = atlas + region Rect2 + margin Rect2, margin restores trim offsets)

Unity manual slicing: Sprite Mode = Multiple, Sprite Editor Slice menu: Automatic, Grid By Cell Size, Grid By Cell Count (with offset/padding); pivot presets or Custom in normalized coords; per-sprite name/rect/pivot/border(9-slice); pixel art wants Pixels Per Unit matched to cell, Filter Mode = Point, Compression = None

libGDX .atlas text format per region: rotate, xy: x,y, size: w,h, orig: origW,origH, offset: left,bottom, index: n (plus split/pad for ninepatch); filenames ending _N store N as index; atlas.findRegions("walk") returns index-ordered frames for new Animation(frameDuration, regions); newer libGDX also reads a compact format (bounds:/offsets:) — write the legacy field-per-line form for max compatibility

Unreal Paper2D: TexturePacker's "UnrealEngine - Paper2d" exporter writes a .paper2dsprites JSON; importing it creates the texture, extracts per-frame Sprite assets, and auto-generates a Flipbook (importer assumes all sprites are animation frames); recommended Border/Shape padding 0 for flipbook workflows

RPG Maker MV/MZ character sheet: per character 3 columns × 4 rows, row order down/left/right/up, middle column = standing pose, outer columns = step frames; default cell 48×48 → single char 144×192, full sheet 8 characters (4 across × 2 down) = 576×384; engine infers cell size (sheet width/12 × height/8; "$"-prefixed = single char, width/3 × height/4), so larger cells work if proportions hold; "!" prefix disables the 6 px vertical lift for doors/objects

LPC universal spritesheet: 64×64 frames, 832×1344 sheet = 13 columns × 21 rows; blocks top-to-bottom: spellcast 7 frames, thrust 8, walk 9 (column 0 = idle stance), slash 6, shoot 13 — each block is 4 direction rows ordered up, left, down, right — plus one hurt/die row of 6 frames; assets dual-licensed GPL 3.0 + CC-BY-SA 3.0 (ImageAI-generated sheets can use the LAYOUT freely; shipping LPC art itself triggers attribution/share-alike)

GIF: max 256 colors per frame (local color tables allow >256 per file), 1-bit transparency (GCE transparent index), delay = 16-bit value in 1/100 s; browsers clamp delays ≤ 1 cs (≤10 ms) to 100 ms, so 2 cs = 20 ms = 50 fps is the practical minimum; disposal methods: 1 = do not dispose, 2 = restore to background, 3 = restore to previous; looping via NETSCAPE2.0 application extension (loop count 0 = infinite)

APNG: acTL (num_frames, num_plays), fcTL per frame (x/y offset, delay_num/delay_den — delay_den 0 means 100, i.e. delays are rational seconds), fdAT data; dispose_op none/background/previous + blend_op source/over; full 8-bit (or 16-bit) alpha; unsupported decoders fall back to the first PNG image; supported by Firefox 3+, Safari 8+, Chrome 59+, Edge — ~96% of browsers

Animated WebP: VP8X + ANIM chunk (background color, 16-bit loop count, 0 = infinite) + one ANMF per frame (frame x/y stored in 2-px units, width/height minus one, 24-bit frame duration in MILLISECONDS, alpha-blend vs overwrite flag, dispose-to-background flag); frames individually lossy or lossless, full alpha either way; canvas max 16383×16383; Chrome 32+, Firefox 65+, Safari 14+; Pillow writes it via save(save_all=True, duration=, loop=)

Minimum internal per-frame metadata superset that projects losslessly onto every format above: sheet rect (x,y,w,h) + rotated flag; trim offset (x,y) + untrimmed sourceSize (w,h); normalized pivot (x,y); duration in integer ms; per-tag: name, from/to frame range, direction (forward/reverse/pingpong/pingpong_reverse), repeat count (0 = infinite); optional: slices/9-patch borders, palette for indexed export, tag color/user-data

feature_ideas.name: Uniform grid sheet export
feature_ideas.description: Compose frames onto a fixed-cell grid PNG with configurable cell size, margin, spacing, columns, and row-per-animation ordering, plus optional power-of-two canvas. Every engine (Unity, Godot, RPG Maker, libGDX) can slice a clean grid, so this is the universal no-metadata fallback.

feature_ideas.name: Aseprite-JSON metadata export
feature_ideas.description: Write json-hash and json-array data files matching Aseprite's export exactly: per-frame frame/rotated/trimmed/spriteSourceSize/sourceSize/duration(ms) and meta.frameTags with direction forward/reverse/pingpong/pingpong_reverse. Unlocks Phaser's load.aseprite + anims.createFromAseprite and every Aseprite-aware tool for free.

feature_ideas.name: TexturePacker-JSON export (hash + array, pivot)
feature_ideas.description: Emit the generic TexturePacker JSON hash/array with normalized per-frame pivot and a PixiJS 'animations' block mapping tag names to frame-name arrays. This one file serves Phaser load.atlas, PixiJS AnimatedSprite, melonJS, PlayCanvas, and most web engines.

feature_ideas.name: Animated GIF export
feature_ideas.description: Per-tag GIF export with palette quantization (256 colors), 1-bit transparency handling against a chosen matte, disposal-method control, and a UI warning that browser floors make 20 ms (50 fps) the minimum reliable frame delay. Right for chat/forum/README previews, wrong for game data.

feature_ideas.name: APNG export
feature_ideas.description: Full-alpha lossless animation with rational per-frame delays (delay_num/delay_den) and a sensible first-frame PNG fallback. The best-looking preview format for sprites with soft alpha edges; ~96% browser support.

feature_ideas.name: Animated WebP export
feature_ideas.description: Smallest web-delivery animation: per-frame millisecond durations, loop count, alpha with per-frame lossy or lossless encoding. Offer lossless as the default for pixel art.

feature_ideas.name: Godot SpriteFrames .tres export
feature_ideas.description: Directly generate a Godot 4 text resource containing AtlasTexture sub-resources (atlas + region + margin restoring trim offsets) and SpriteFrames animations with per-animation FPS, loop flag, and per-frame duration multipliers converted from millisecond timings. Godot has no native JSON atlas import, so this saves users the manual grid-slice step entirely.
feature_ideas.depends_on: internal frame metadata model; ms-to-FPS/multiplier conversion

feature_ideas.name: Engine export preset picker
feature_ideas.description: A single dropdown (Unity, Godot 4, Phaser 3, PixiJS, Unreal Paper2D, libGDX, RPG Maker MZ, LPC, Web preview) that pre-selects format, grid vs packed layout, padding, pivot convention, and file naming, with a short 'how to import' note per engine. Removes the format-knowledge burden from users.

feature_ideas.name: RPG Maker MV/MZ character sheet preset
feature_ideas.description: Assemble walk cycles into the 3x4 (down/left/right/up, middle column idle) layout at 48x48 or custom cell size, emitting either a $-prefixed single-character sheet (144x192) or a full 4x2 eight-character sheet (576x384), with the ! prefix option for objects. Correct proportions matter because the engine infers cell size from sheet dimensions.
feature_ideas.depends_on: grid sheet export; direction-aware animation tagging

feature_ideas.name: Trim + packed-atlas assembly
feature_ideas.description: Trim transparent borders per frame, record trim offsets (spriteSourceSize) and untrimmed sourceSize, and pack with a MaxRects-style algorithm (rotation off by default for compatibility, optional 90-degree rotation with the rotated flag). Cuts texture memory heavily for character animation frames.
feature_ideas.depends_on: internal frame metadata model; a rectpack library or in-repo MaxRects

feature_ideas.name: Internal frame metadata model + project sidecar
feature_ideas.description: A dataclass model tracking, per frame: sheet rect, rotated, trim offset, sourceSize, normalized pivot, duration in ms; per tag: name, range, direction, repeat; plus slices and palette. Persist it in the Sprite tab's project JSON (matching ImageAI's sidecar convention) so every exporter is a pure projection of one source of truth.

feature_ideas.name: Pivot/anchor editor
feature_ideas.description: Set a pivot per tag or per frame by clicking on the frame (with presets: center, bottom-center for platformer feet), stored normalized 0-1 and exported as TexturePacker pivot, Phaser anchor, or baked into grid alignment. Consistent pivots are what stop sprites from 'sliding' between animation frames in-engine.

feature_ideas.name: Animation preview player
feature_ideas.description: In-tab playback honoring per-frame millisecond durations and loop modes (forward, reverse, pingpong), with tag selection, onion-skin overlay, and a checkerboard alpha background. Users must validate timing before export because engines will reproduce exactly what the metadata says.

feature_ideas.name: LPC universal sheet preset
feature_ideas.description: Assemble generated walk/slash/thrust/cast/bow/hurt actions into the standard 832x1344 LPC layout (64x64 cells, 4 direction rows up/left/down/right per action, fixed frame counts). Instantly compatible with the large LPC tooling ecosystem; note the layout is free to use while LPC art assets are GPL 3.0 + CC-BY-SA 3.0.

feature_ideas.name: libGDX .atlas export
feature_ideas.description: Write the legacy line-based .atlas text format (xy/size/orig/offset/rotate/index per region) using name_N index suffixes so atlas.findRegions(name) returns ordered animation frames. Covers libGDX and the Godot/LittleKt importers that read the same format.

feature_ideas.name: Starling/Sparrow XML + cocos2d plist export
feature_ideas.description: Generic XML TextureAtlas (SubTexture entries with x/y/width/height/frameX/frameY) and cocos2d-style plist for older toolchains. Low effort once the metadata model exists, but niche demand.

feature_ideas.name: Unreal Paper2D .paper2dsprites export
feature_ideas.description: Emit the Paper2D JSON descriptor so Unreal auto-creates the texture, per-frame Sprite assets, and a Flipbook on import. Use zero border/shape padding per the Paper2D workflow recommendation.

feature_ideas.name: Native .aseprite file writer
feature_ideas.description: Write a real .aseprite file (header magic 0xA5E0; Layer 0x2004, zlib Cel 0x2005, Tags 0x2018, Palette 0x2019, Slice 0x2022 chunks) with one layer, one cel per frame, and tags with loop directions. Payoff: Unity's official com.unity.2d.aseprite importer consumes it directly (frames to clips, tags, timings), and users get lossless round-trip editing in Aseprite; moderate binary-format effort, pure-Python feasible (struct + zlib).

feature_ideas.name: Duration-to-FPS reconciliation helper
feature_ideas.description: When a target (Godot animation FPS, GIF centisecond delays, fixed-FPS engines) cannot express arbitrary millisecond durations, compute the best base FPS (GCD of durations) and per-frame multipliers or repeats, and show the user the rounding error before export.

summary:
Sprite sizing follows hardware history. 8x8 is the hardware tile unit on NES/Game Boy/Master System; playable characters there are metasprites of 16x16 (small NES Mario, Game Boy heroes) to 16x32. The 16-bit era (SNES/Genesis) uses 16x16 to 32x32 characters built from 8x8 4bpp tiles, with SNES hardware sprite sizes of 8x8, 16x16, 32x32, and 64x64. 24x24 and 16x24 are common JRPG field-sprite sizes; 48x48 is the RPG Maker MV/MZ grid; 64x64 covers large characters and bosses; 96x96-128x128 covers fighting-game and "large HD" characters (CPS-2/SNK fighters are ~100-200 px tall). Tiles standardize on 8x8 (8-bit), 16x16 (16-bit and modern indie default), 32x32, and 48x48 (RPG Maker). Modern "HD pixel art" games pick a 16:9 canvas that integer-scales to 1080p: 320x180 (x6, Celeste), 384x216 (x5), 480x270 (x4, Hyper Light Drifter), 640x360 (x3); Shovel Knight uses 400x240. So the Sprite tab should offer a size-preset dropdown (8/16/24/32/48/64/96/128 + rectangular 16x32, 16x24, 32x64) with era/genre labels, plus a canvas/integer-scale calculator.

Animation timing in pixel art is per-frame milliseconds, not a global fps. Aseprite is the reference tool: each frame stores a WORD duration in milliseconds in the frame header (default 100 ms = 10 fps; the old file-header "speed" field is deprecated), and its exported JSON sheet data carries `"duration"` per frame plus `frameTags`. Conventional rates: 12 fps is the community default ("animating on twos" = every other frame of 24 fps film; "on threes" = 8 fps); walk cycles use 4/6/8 frames at ~10-12 fps; idles run slower (150-300 ms holds); attacks mix long anticipation holds (100-200 ms) with 1-2 fast strike frames (30-70 ms). GIF export quantizes delays to centiseconds and browsers clamp tiny delays, so a GIF preview needs a rounding warning. Color counts also follow hardware: Game Boy = 4 shades (3 + transparent for objects, BGP/OBP0/OBP1 registers); NES = 64-entry master palette, 8 palettes x 3 colors + shared backdrop = ~25 simultaneous colors (sprites get 4 palettes of 3 + transparent); SNES = 8 sprite palettes of 15 colors + transparent index 0, from 256-entry CGRAM, 15-bit BGR (32,768 colors); Genesis = 4 palettes x 15+1 from 512. Modern norms are 8-32 colors per character. Limiting colors is what makes AI output read as one style: it forces shared ramps across all action clips, kills per-frame quantization flicker, and enables palette-swap variants.

Palette file formats are all small and easy to implement. GIMP .gpl: text; line 1 `GIMP Palette`, optional `Name: `, optional `Columns: ` (0-255), `#` comments, then `R G B name` with 0-255 ints. JASC .pal: text; `JASC-PAL`, `0100`, color count (e.g. 256), then `R G B` lines 0-255. Adobe .act: raw binary, 768 bytes = 256 RGB triples; optional 4-byte footer = 2-byte color count + 2-byte transparency index (772 bytes total). Adobe .aco: big-endian binary; v1 = version word, count word, then per color a 2-byte colorspace ID (0=RGB, 1=HSB, 2=CMYK, 7=Lab, 8=Grayscale) + four 16-bit components (RGB scaled 0-65535); v2 appends a 4-byte length + UTF-16BE name per color. Adobe .ase: big-endian; signature `ASEF`, version 2x int16 (1.0), int32 block count; blocks 0xC001 group start / 0xC002 group end / 0x0001 color entry; color entry = name, 4-char model (`RGB `, `CMYK`, `LAB `, `Gray`), float32 components, int16 type (0 global, 1 spot, 2 normal). paint.net .txt: text, up to 96 colors, one `AARRGGBB` hex per line, `;` comments. Lospec .hex: one bare RRGGBB per line, no `#`. Lospec also has a free JSON API — `https://lospec.com/palette-list/{slug}.json` returns `{name, author, colors:[hex...]}` (plus a .csv variant and a `lospec-palette://` URI scheme) — ideal for a built-in curated-palette browser over its ~4,400 palettes with color-count and tag filters.

Transparency and rendering conventions: modern output is PNG RGBA with binary alpha (0 or 255 — crisp pixel art avoids semi-transparent edge pixels, so chroma-keyed AI frames must be alpha-thresholded). Legacy color-key uses magenta #FF00FF (chosen because it is RGB/BGR-symmetric and almost never appears in art) or green; indexed formats use palette index 0 as transparent (NES/SNES/GB hardware, GIF transparent-color index, old engines like SDL SetColorKey / DirectDraw / RPG Maker 2000-2003). A colorkey/index-0 export option is still needed for retro engines, homebrew, and GIF. Scaling must be nearest-neighbor at integer factors only; the project's "scaled proportionally, never cropped or distorted" rule maps cleanly onto pixel art: downscale AI frames to the sprite grid at the largest integer-fitting size, then center-pad with transparent pixels to fill the cell (same pattern as the existing Gemini reference-image handling) — never stretch to the cell. Dithering: error-diffusion (Floyd-Steinberg) produces per-frame noise that shimmers ("dither crawl") across animation frames, so quantization should default to no dither, offer ordered/Bayer (2x2/4x4/8x8) as an option, and warn against error diffusion for animations. Outlines are a style choice: none, solid black, or "sel-out" (selective outline — outline shaded relative to the adjacent fill, lighter where the form catches light); a simple auto-darken outline pass is enough for v1.
key_facts: Character sprite size presets that match real conventions: 8x8 (tile unit / ultra-low-res), 16x16 (NES/GB heroes, small Mario), 16x32 (big NES Mario), 16x24/24x24 (JRPG field sprites), 32x32 (SNES/Genesis + modern indie default), 48x48 (RPG Maker MV/MZ grid), 64x64 (large chars/bosses), 96x96-128x128 (fighting-game scale).

SNES hardware sprite sizes: 8x8, 16x16, 32x32, 64x64 (plus 16x32, 32x64 rectangles); all sprites are 4bpp = 15 colors + transparent index 0, selecting one of 8 sprite palettes in the upper half of 256-entry CGRAM; master color space is 15-bit BGR (32,768 colors).

NES: 64-entry master palette (~54 visually distinct); 4 background + 4 sprite palettes of 3 colors each plus one shared backdrop color = ~25 simultaneous colors; entry 0 of every sprite palette is transparent; hardware sprites are 8x8 or 8x16.
Game Boy (DMG): 4 shades via BGP/OBP0/OBP1 registers; object color 0 is always transparent so sprites get 3 usable shades. Game Boy Color: 8 BG + 8 OBJ palettes, 4 colors each, RGB555 15-bit color.

Modern HD-pixel canvas presets are 16:9 integer divisors of 1920x1080: 320x180 (x6, Celeste), 384x216 (x5), 480x270 (x4, Hyper Light Drifter), 640x360 (x3); Shovel Knight uses 400x240. Tiles: 8x8, 16x16 (modern default), 32x32, 48x48.

Aseprite stores animation timing as per-frame duration: a WORD in milliseconds in each frame header of the .aseprite/.ase file; the file-header 'speed' WORD is DEPRECATED in favor of per-frame durations; default frame duration is 100 ms (10 fps).
Aseprite color depths: 32bpp RGBA, 16bpp grayscale, 8bpp indexed; new palette chunk 0x2019 supports per-color alpha, old chunk 0x0004 is RGB-only max 256 colors.

Pixel-art timing conventions: 12 fps community default = 'animating on twos' (half of 24 fps film); 'on threes' = 8 fps; walk cycles are 4/6/8 frames at ~10-12 fps; key poses hold 3-4 frames, transitions 1-2 frames; one indie guide default is 10 fps (= Aseprite's 100 ms).
GIF stores frame delay in centiseconds (10 ms steps) and browsers clamp very small delays, so per-frame ms durations get rounded on GIF export — show a warning.

GIMP .gpl format: line 1 magic 'GIMP Palette'; optional 'Name: <utf-8>'; optional 'Columns: <0-255>' (0 = variable); '#' starts a comment; color lines are 'R G B optional name' with integers 0-255, sRGB, no alpha.
JASC .pal format: line 1 'JASC-PAL', line 2 version '0100', line 3 color count (e.g. '256'), then one 'R G B' line per color, values 0-255, space-separated.
Adobe .act format: raw binary, 768 bytes = 256 x 3 bytes RGB in order; optional 4-byte footer makes 772 bytes: 2-byte number of colors then 2-byte transparency color index (both big-endian).

Adobe .aco format: big-endian; v1 = uint16 version(1), uint16 count, then per color uint16 colorspace (0=RGB, 1=HSB, 2=CMYK, 7=Lab, 8=Grayscale) + 4 x uint16 components with RGB scaled 0-65535 (divide by 257 for 8-bit); v2 block repeats colors and appends uint32 name length + UTF-16BE name; files often contain v1 then v2 blocks.

Adobe .ase (Swatch Exchange): big-endian; signature 'ASEF'; version 2 x int16 (1, 0); int32 block count; block types 0xC001 group start, 0xC002 group end, 0x0001 color entry; color entry carries UTF-16BE name, 4-char color model ('RGB ', 'CMYK', 'LAB ', 'Gray'), float32 components (RGB 3 floats 0.0-1.0), and int16 color type (0=global, 1=spot, 2=normal).
paint.net palette .txt: plain text, up to 96 colors (missing slots fill with FFFFFFFF), one 8-hex-digit AARRGGBB per line, lines starting with ';' are comments.

Lospec .hex download: one bare RRGGBB hex string per line, no '#' prefix. Lospec palette API: GET https://lospec.com/palette-list/{slug}.json returns {"name", "author", "colors": ["574368", ...]}; .csv variant = name,author,hex,hex,...; 404 returns {error: "file not found"}; lospec-palette:// URI scheme exists for app registration; ~4,433 palettes, filterable by exact/max/min color count and tags (e.g. 'hardware', 'gameboy').

Magenta #FF00FF is the classic colorkey because it is symmetric in RGB vs BGR and almost never occurs in real art; SDL_SetColorKey/DirectDraw DDBLT_KEYSRC are the legacy consumers; indexed formats use palette index 0 (or GIF transparent color index) as transparent.
Crisp pixel-art convention: binary alpha only (0 or 255) — chroma-keyed AI frames have soft alpha edges that must be thresholded, and colorkey export requires no semi-transparent pixels at all.

Scaling rules: nearest-neighbor only, integer factors only (set 'integer scale' in engines); the project's no-crop/no-distort rule maps to: downscale to the largest integer-fitting size inside the sprite cell, center on a transparent canvas of the cell size — same pattern as the existing Gemini reference-image aspect handling.
Sprite-sheet hygiene: keep a 1 px transparent border/padding (or edge extrusion) around each frame to prevent texture bleeding at scale.

Error-diffusion dithering (Floyd-Steinberg) is temporally unstable across animation frames (dither crawl); default quantization for sprites should be dither=none, with optional ordered/Bayer 2x2/4x4/8x8; Pillow's Image.quantize supports MEDIANCUT/MAXCOVERAGE/FASTOCTREE methods and Dither.NONE vs FLOYDSTEINBERG.

Sel-out (selective outlining) = outline shaded relative to the neighboring fill color — darker where the form is dark, lighter where lit — instead of a uniform black outline; a stylistic option, not a default.
Aseprite's exported JSON sheet data (--data) carries frames[].duration in ms and meta.frameTags [{name, from, to, direction}] — the natural interchange target for per-action animation tags.

feature_ideas.description: Preset character/tile sizes (8, 16, 16x24, 24, 16x32, 32, 48, 64, 96, 128 px) labeled by era/genre (NES hero, SNES/indie standard, RPG Maker 48x48 grid, fighting-game large). Sets the target cell size that the whole downstream pipeline quantizes and pads to.

feature_ideas.name: Animated GIF/APNG preview export with timing warning

feature_ideas.name: Chroma key with tolerance slider, local or cloud

key_facts: Aseprite CLI sheet export flags: --sheet, --data, --format (json-hash default | json-array), --sheet-type (horizontal|vertical|rows|columns|packed), --split-layers, --split-tags, --split-slices, --border-padding, --shape-padding, --inner-padding, --trim.
Aseprite filename-format placeholders: {title}, {layer}, {tag}, {frame}, padded {frame01}/{frame000}, {tagframe} (frame index within the current tag), {extension}.
Aseprite tag animation directions are exactly three: Forward, Reverse, Ping-pong; tags carry a name and are created via Frame > Tags > New Tag (F2).
Aseprite slices (Slice tool, Shift+C) store bounds, an optional 9-patch center rectangle, and a per-slice pivot; all are emitted in the sprite-sheet JSON 'slices' section.
Aseprite onion skinning toggles with F3; configuration (previous/next frame counts, red/blue tint) lives under the Configure Timeline icon.
Aseprite license: GPLv2 until 2016-08-26, then a proprietary EULA — source-available, personal compile allowed, redistribution forbidden; NOT open source.
LibreSprite is GPL-2.0, forked from Aseprite's last GPLv2 commit; features: real-time animation preview, onion skinning, built-in + custom palettes, layers/frames, tiled drawing mode.
Piskel is Apache-2.0 (web + desktop Win/macOS/Linux); live preview with on-the-fly frame-delay adjustment; exports animated GIF, PNG spritesheet, and ZIP of PNGs; uses gif.js/supergif/jszip.

Pixelorama is MIT, built on Godot 4.7.1; timeline has frame tags, onion skinning, audio synchronization, and draw-while-playing; exports PNG, animated PNG (APNG), spritesheets, GIF, and video; has CLI bulk-export automation and per-layer/frame/cel user metadata.

Pro Motion NG (commercial + feature-limited Free Edition): sprite-sheet read/write (PNG/BMP), palette-based color cycling, 25+ paint modes, onion skinning/light table, tile-map engine, palette editor with range operations; formats gif/bmp/png/tga/fli/flc.

GraphicsGale became freeware 2017-06-18 (Windows, v2.11.03); real-time animation preview while editing; onion skin shows previous AND next frames; native .gal format; imports/exports .ico/.gif/.avi/.cur/.ani; exports sprite sheets or per-frame files.

TexturePacker Pro: $49.99 perpetual single-user license with 1 year of updates (Win/macOS/Linux + CI/Docker); packing algorithms Grid, Basic, MaxRects, Polygon; trim + alias detection (identical-sprite dedup); multipack; 9-patch; pivot-point editor with animation preview; 48+ data exporters (Unity, Godot, Phaser, libGDX, Unreal, generic JSON/XML); image outputs incl. PNG-8 (pngquant), WebP, KTX, PVR/PVRTC, ETC1/ETC2, DXT1/DXT5, ASTC, Basis; Zopfli compression.

ShoeBox (free, Adobe AIR, Win/macOS) tool list: Pack Sprites, Read Sprites, Extract Sprites, Ani Frames (GIF/SWF/PNG-sequence to frames), Frame Sheet, Bitmap Font (AngelCode .fnt), Split PSD, Extract Tiles, Texture Ripper, Sprite Pivots (bulk pivot editing), Slice 9, Mask Image.

Free Texture Packer is MIT; web app + desktop (Win/Mac/Linux) + CLI/webpack/gulp/grunt modules; exporters: json (hash/array), xml, css, pixi.js, godot, phaser, cocos2d; features rotation, trim, multipack, detect-identical, TinyPNG, split-sheet tool; custom exporters via mustache templates receiving rects/config/appInfo.

Spritely (video-to-spritesheet, $30 one-time after 5 free exports): click-any-color chroma key with tolerance slider 0 (precise) to 150 (aggressive); every-Nth-frame extraction; default 30 FPS; start/end range; canvas presets 24–1024 px; left/center/right + top/center/bottom positioning; optional halo removal; transparent-PNG sheet or ZIP output.

Nim.video Animate Studio has no public docs; observed UI (from maintainer): per-action prompt cards (attack_jump, idle_ready, walk_forward, hurt, shield_block, sword_attack, walk; 1–15 s; 'seamless loop, no camera movement, no new shadows'), model picker (Imagine 1.5 / Wan 2.7, 720p), 'FRAMES: Every 8' extraction, 'Corridor Key' vs 'Chroma Key' toggle, CHROMA color picker, TOL tolerance slider, Cloud/Local processing, 'Remove background' button.

AI-adjacent ecosystem: PixelLab (pixellab.ai) ships a web app AND an Aseprite plugin with text-prompt generation, skeleton-based animation control, up-to-8-direction character generation, inpainting, and sprite-sheet output; Aseprite and Pixelorama themselves ship no AI features.

Table-stakes derived from the survey: frame strip (reorder/duplicate/delete/per-frame ms duration), named action tags with forward/reverse/ping-pong loop modes, FPS-controlled looping preview with pixel-grid zoom, chroma key with color pick + tolerance, Nth-frame extraction, grid sheet export with border/shape/inner padding + trim, Aseprite-compatible JSON (json-hash/json-array with frameTags), per-tag export with {tag}_{frame} filename templates, GIF export, sheet import/slicing, and a project file with metadata.

Deferrable power-user extras: MaxRects/polygon packed atlases, multipack, extrude/rotation, alias dedup, 9-patch slices and per-sprite pivot editors, palette remap/.gpl/.pal round-trip, APNG/WebP/video export, engine-specific exporters beyond 1-2, color cycling, tilemaps, bitmap fonts, onion-skin drawing tools.
summary:
Across the six editors and three packers surveyed, a remarkably stable feature core repeats. Every animation-capable editor (Aseprite, LibreSprite, Piskel, Pixelorama, GraphicsGale, Pro Motion NG) ships: a frame timeline with reorder/duplicate/delete and per-frame duration in milliseconds; a real-time looping preview with FPS/delay control; onion skinning; layers; a palette panel; and both animated-GIF and sprite-sheet export. Aseprite defines the interchange conventions the whole ecosystem copies: named frame tags with exactly three loop directions (Forward, Reverse, Ping-pong), sheet types horizontal/vertical/rows/columns/packed, three padding knobs (border/shape/inner) plus trim, JSON metadata in json-hash or json-array form carrying frameTags and durations, and filename templates with {tag}/{frame}/{frame01}/{tagframe} placeholders. Its slices add 9-patch centers and per-slice pivots to the JSON. Licensing splits the field: Aseprite is proprietary source-available (EULA since 2016), LibreSprite (GPL-2.0), Piskel (Apache-2.0), Pixelorama (MIT), and Free Texture Packer (MIT) are open, GraphicsGale is freeware, Pro Motion NG and TexturePacker ($49.99 perpetual) are commercial with free tiers.

The packers show what "export done well" means beyond a grid: TexturePacker's Grid/Basic/MaxRects/Polygon algorithms, trim with alias (duplicate-sprite) detection, extrude, multipack, pivot-point editing with animation preview, 48+ engine exporters, and compressed image outputs (PNG-8/WebP/KTX/PVR/ETC/ASTC); Free Texture Packer covers the open-source subset (json/xml/css/pixi.js/godot/phaser/cocos2d plus mustache-template custom exporters); ShoeBox contributes the utility checklist our pipeline actually needs — extract sprites from sheets, convert GIF/sequences to frames, bulk pivot editing, 9-slice. Since we generate frames rather than draw them, the packer feature set matters more to us than the drawing feature set.

The AI-adjacent field validates the exact Nim-style pipeline we plan. Spritely ($30 one-time) is a shipping video-to-spritesheet product whose controls map 1:1 onto Nim's: click-to-pick chroma color, tolerance slider 0-150, every-Nth-frame extraction, 30 FPS default, canvas presets 24-1024 px, anchor positioning, and halo removal. PixelLab ships AI pixel-art generation with skeleton-based animation, 8-direction characters, and inpainting — notably as an Aseprite plugin, showing AI slots into existing sprite workflows rather than replacing them. Aseprite and Pixelorama themselves have added no AI features. Nim's Animate Studio remains undocumented publicly; the maintainer's UI observations (prompt cards per action, Imagine 1.5/Wan 2.7 at 720p, FRAMES: Every 8, Corridor Key vs Chroma Key, TOL, Cloud/Local) are the only spec.

Conclusion — table-stakes for a credible sprite tool given our generate-then-process scope: frame strip management (reorder/duplicate/delete, per-frame ms), named action tags with forward/reverse/ping-pong, an FPS-controlled looping preview with pixel-grid zoom and checkerboard alpha, chroma key (color pick + tolerance, local processing), Nth-frame/FPS/range extraction, auto-trim, grid sheet export with the three Aseprite padding knobs, Aseprite-compatible JSON (json-hash/json-array + frameTags), per-tag export with {tag}_{frame} templates, GIF export, sheet import/slicing (to round-trip Nano Banana sheet output), and a project file with provenance metadata. Deferrable power-user extras: MaxRects/polygon packing, multipack, extrude/rotation, alias dedup, pivot/9-patch editors, palette remap and .gpl/.pal round-trip, APNG/WebP, engine exporters beyond Godot/Phaser, color cycling, tilemaps, bitmap fonts, and any hand-drawing tools — the editors already own that ground, and interop (their JSON formats) beats reimplementation.

The Nim.video "Animate Studio" pipeline the screenshot shows is fully reproducible from public parts. Its "Corridor Key" toggle refers to CorridorKey, an open-source neural green-screen keyer that Niko Pueringer of Corridor Digital released in early 2026 (GitHub: nikopueringer/CorridorKey, 14.6k stars). Unlike a plain color-distance chroma key, CorridorKey takes the RGB footage plus a coarse alpha hint and predicts the true un-multiplied foreground color and a clean linear alpha per pixel, so motion blur, hair, and translucent edges survive. It runs locally on 6-8 GB VRAM (CUDA/ROCm/MPS/MLX), outputs linear EXR (Matte/FG/Processed folders), and carries a custom CC BY-NC-SA-style license: processing images for commercial projects is allowed, but repackaging it or selling inference as a paid API is not (commercial integration requires an agreement with Corridor). Nim's other model choices check out too: "Imagine 1.5" is xAI's grok-imagine-video-1.5 (1-15 s clips at 24 fps, 480p/720p/1080p, image-to-video with references — matching the 1-15 s per-action cards), and Wan 2.7 is Alibaba's April-2026 Apache-2.0 open-weights release (27B MoE, up to 1080p/15 s); Wan 2.2 (Apache-2.0, 720p@24fps, I2V-A14B) runs a 5 s clip on a single 24 GB consumer GPU.

Dedicated sprite generators split into pixel-art-native and general tools. summary:
Classic chroma keying is best implemented as color-distance keying in YCbCr (YCrCb in OpenCV), not RGB/HSV thresholding: convert with cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2YCrCb), measure Euclidean distance in the (Cr,Cb) chroma plane from the key color, and map distance through a two-threshold ramp — dist < tol_a gives alpha 0, dist > tol_b gives alpha 255, linear (or smoothstep) in between. Keying on chroma only ignores luminance, so wrinkles/shadows in an AI-generated green field key cleanly; HSV inRange (green hue roughly 40–80 in OpenCV's 0–179 H scale) works as a quick mode but breaks on dark greens. ffmpeg (already bundled by the app) provides the same thing as filters: chromakey (YUV-space; options color, similarity 0.01–1.0, blend 0.0–1.0 where blend>0 yields graded alpha), colorkey (RGB-space equivalent), and a despill filter (type green|blue, mix = spillmap generation, expand = residual spill removal, per-channel red/green/blue with green=-1 for greenscreen, brightness, alpha). Despill in Python is per-pixel green clamping — the canonical expressions are g>(r+b)/2?(r+b)/2:g (average), g>(2*b+r)/3 (double-blue average), g>r?r:g / g>b?b:g (limit variants); compute the spill matte as the difference between original and despilled, desaturate it, and add it back to restore edge luminance. Anti-aliased edges from AI images are mixed pixels: after soft-ramp alpha + despill, apply color decontamination F=(C−(1−α)·K)/α, then choke (cv2.erode on the mask) and feather (cv2.GaussianBlur on alpha), with morphological open for despeckle.

For AI matting, rembg (MIT, Python >=3.11 <3.14, pip install "rembg[cpu]" pulling onnxruntime which is MIT with wheels on all desktop platforms) is the practical desktop choice. Verified ONNX weights from its release assets: u2netp 4.4 MB (fast, lowest quality), silueta 42.1 MB, u2net 167.8 MB, isnet-general-use 170.4 MB, isnet-anime 167.9 MB (best fit for cel/sprite content), birefnet-general-lite 213.6 MB, birefnet-general 927.6 MB, bria-rmbg-2.0 976.9 MB (BRIA license — paid agreement for commercial use; avoid as default). API: new_session(model_name) + remove(data, session=..., alpha_matting=True, alpha_matting_foreground_threshold=240, alpha_matting_background_threshold=10, alpha_matting_erode_size=10, post_process_mask, only_mask, bgcolor); models auto-download to ~/.rembg/models/. CPU reality: u2net/isnet run ~1–3 s per frame; BiRefNet-class models take several seconds to ~15 s per frame on CPU (transparent-background/InSPyReNet benchmarks at ~16.5 s/image CPU) — fine for a batch job with a progress bar, not for live preview. transparent-background (MIT, InSPyReNet ACCV 2022) is an alternative but drags in full PyTorch; rembg's onnxruntime path is lighter for ImageAI. Interactive segmentation: rembg ships SAM (vit_b encoder 342.6 MB, quantized 103.8 MB) and mobile_sam (encoder 26.9 MB, quantized 10.5 MB) with point/box prompts — MobileSAM is the only variant comfortably interactive on CPU (~10M params, near-SAM quality at mIoU ~0.74). ViTMatte trimap-matting ONNX models (vitmatte-small 109.1 MB) also sit in rembg's release assets for edge-quality refinement.

Frame extraction: every-Nth-frame is -vf "select='not(mod(n,8))'" with -fps_mode vfr (formerly -vsync vfr — without it ffmpeg duplicates frames to fill a constant-rate output); n is the zero-based frame number. fps=12 resamples to a constant rate instead (decodes everything, duplicates/drops as needed) — better when the user thinks in "output FPS" rather than "every 8th frame"; select+vfr is faster for sparse pulls. Scene-aware extraction uses select='gt(scene,0.4)' (scene is a 0–1 new-scene likelihood) or PySceneDetect (BSD-3-Clause, detect(path, ContentDetector(threshold=27.0)), backends OpenCV/PyAV/MoviePy, and it can auto-use imageio-ffmpeg's bundled binary). Since ImageAI already owns core/video/ffmpeg_utils.py, extraction should reuse it; imageio-ffmpeg (BSD-2-Clause, ~60 MiB wheels bundling ffmpeg 7.x) and PyAV (binary wheels bundle FFmpeg libs) remain pip-only fallbacks. Frame cleanup: auto-crop via the alpha channel (cv2.findNonZero + cv2.boundingRect, or PIL getbbox) but take the union bbox across an action's frames, then re-pad to a uniform canvas anchored bottom-center so feet stay planted; de-jitter with skimage.registration.phase_cross_correlation(ref, moving, upsample_factor=10) for 1/10-pixel translation estimates applied via scipy.ndimage.shift or cv2.warpAffine — run it on the alpha masks (not RGB) so background drift can't bias the shift; alpha-centroid alignment (cv2.moments: cx=m10/m00) is the cheap fallback and the right tool when limbs move but the body core should stay fixed. Background drift itself is best neutralized by keying/matting each frame independently, or by median-stacking frames to estimate the static background and differencing.

"Corridor Key" is real and documented: CorridorKey by Niko Pueringer (Corridor Digital), released Feb 2026, github.com/nikopueringer/CorridorKey. It is a two-stage pipeline — an alpha-hint model (GVM, VideoMaMa, or BiRefNet) produces a coarse mask, then a ~300 MB neural "unmixer" checkpoint predicts straight (unpremultiplied) foreground color and linear alpha per pixel at native 2048×2048, handling hair/motion-blur/translucency, with a classic despill-strength (0–10) post filter. Crucially for ImageAI: it is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (commercial incorporation requires permission), not pip-installable (uv-managed clone), and wants 6–8 GB VRAM minimum — so it cannot be embedded, but its *technique* (matting model for alpha hint + unmix/decontaminate against the estimated key color + despill) is exactly reproducible with rembg/isnet-anime + the decontamination formula above, and Nim's "Corridor Key" toggle is almost certainly this style of ML matting versus classic chroma distance.
key_facts: Classic keyer: convert BGR->YCrCb (cv2.COLOR_BGR2YCrCb), alpha from Euclidean distance in the (Cr,Cb) plane to the key color's (Cr,Cb); two thresholds tol_a (fully transparent below) and tol_b (fully opaque above) with a linear/smoothstep ramp between = Nim-style TOL + softness controls
HSV quick-key: cv2.inRange on H around 40-80 (OpenCV H is 0-179), S and V floors ~40; fails on dark/desaturated greens where YCbCr distance still works

Canonical despill expressions: average g>(r+b)/2?(r+b)/2:g; double-blue (2*b+r)/3; double-red (b+2*r)/3; blue-limit g>b?b:g; red-limit g>r?r:g (Ben McEwan, benmcewan.com/blog/understanding-despill-algorithms)
Luminance restore after despill: diff = original - despilled, desaturate diff to grayscale, add back to despilled result (prevents darkened edges)
Edge decontamination for anti-aliased AI edges: F = (C - (1-alpha)*K) / alpha where K is the key color (unmix/unpremultiply); apply only where 0<alpha<1
Edge choke = cv2.erode on binary mask (1-2 px kernel); feather = cv2.GaussianBlur on the alpha channel; despeckle = cv2.morphologyEx MORPH_OPEN; these three map to a minimal 'edge' control group

ffmpeg chromakey filter: YUV-space; options color, similarity (0.01=exact color only .. 1.0=everything), blend (0.0=binary alpha, >0=graded transparency), yuv flag; colorkey is the RGB-space twin; both usable through the app's existing core/video/ffmpeg_utils.py
ffmpeg despill filter options: type=green|blue, mix (spillmap generation), expand (residual spill removal), red/green/blue channel controls (green should be -1 for greenscreen), brightness, alpha
rembg: MIT license, Python >=3.11,<3.14, install as pip install "rembg[cpu]" (onnxruntime) or "rembg[gpu]" (onnxruntime-gpu); models auto-download to ~/.rembg/models/

rembg API: new_session(model_name); remove(input, session=..., alpha_matting=True, alpha_matting_foreground_threshold=240, alpha_matting_background_threshold=10, alpha_matting_erode_size=10, post_process_mask=..., only_mask=..., bgcolor=...)

Verified rembg model ONNX sizes (GitHub release v0.0.0 assets): u2netp 4.4 MB, silueta 42.1 MB, u2net 167.8 MB, u2net_human_seg 167.8 MB, isnet-anime 167.9 MB, isnet-general-use 170.4 MB, birefnet-general-lite 213.6 MB, birefnet-general 927.6 MB, BiRefNet_HR-general 1048 MB, bria-rmbg-2.0 976.9 MB
isnet-anime is the model to default for cel/sprite-style characters; bria-rmbg (RMBG-2.0) requires a paid BRIA license for commercial use — do not make it the default

SAM in rembg: sam_vit_b encoder 342.6 MB (quant 103.8 MB) + decoder 15.7 MB, mobile_sam encoder 26.9 MB (quant 10.5 MB); supports point and box prompts; MobileSAM (~10M params, mIoU ~0.74, ~2-4 pts below full SAM) is the only CPU-interactive variant
ViTMatte trimap-matting ONNX models exist in rembg's release assets: vitmatte-small-composition-1k 109.1 MB, vitmatte-base 379.5 MB

transparent-background (InSPyReNet): MIT license, modes base [1024x1024] / fast [384x384] / base-nightly, Remover(mode=..., device=..., ckpt=...).process(img, type='rgba'|'map'|'green'|'blur'|'overlay', threshold=...); requires full PyTorch (torch>=1.7.1, torchvision, timm, kornia); ~16.5 s/image CPU inference benchmark
BiRefNet upstream (ZhengPeng7/BiRefNet) is MIT licensed; CPU inference is seconds-per-image, 17 FPS at 1024x1024 only on an RTX 4090 FP16

Every-Nth-frame extraction: -vf "select='not(mod(n,8))'" -fps_mode vfr out_%04d.png (n = zero-based frame number; -fps_mode vfr replaces deprecated -vsync vfr; omitting it duplicates frames to fill CFR output)
FPS resampling: -vf fps=12 decodes all frames and duplicates/drops to a constant rate; select+vfr is faster for sparse extraction, fps= matches a 'target FPS' mental model

Scene-aware extraction: -vf "select='gt(scene,0.4)'" (scene = 0-1 new-scene likelihood), or PySceneDetect (BSD-3-Clause): detect(path, ContentDetector(threshold=27.0)); backends OpenCV/PyAV/MoviePy and it can use imageio-ffmpeg's bundled binary

imageio-ffmpeg: BSD-2-Clause, wheels ~60 MiB bundling the ffmpeg binary (7.x) for win x86-64, macOS arm64/x86-64, manylinux x86-64/aarch64; irrelevant here since ImageAI already bundles ffmpeg via core/video/ffmpeg_utils.py but is the pip-only fallback

Auto-crop: bbox from alpha via cv2.findNonZero(alpha)+cv2.boundingRect (or PIL Image.getbbox()); use the UNION bbox across all frames of one action, then re-pad every frame to one uniform canvas anchored bottom-center so the sprite's feet stay planted

De-jitter: skimage.registration.phase_cross_correlation(reference_image, moving_image, upsample_factor=10) registers to 1/upsample_factor pixel; apply shift with scipy.ndimage.shift or cv2.warpAffine; run on alpha masks so background drift cannot bias the estimate; alpha-centroid (cv2.moments m10/m00, m01/m00) is the cheap fallback

CorridorKey (github.com/nikopueringer/CorridorKey, Niko Pueringer/Corridor Digital, Feb 2026): two-stage = alpha hint (GVM BSD-2-Clause / VideoMaMa CC BY-NC-4.0 / BiRefNet) -> ~300 MB neural unmixer predicting straight FG color + linear alpha at 2048x2048; despill strength 0-10; outputs EXR matte/FG/premult

CorridorKey license is CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 (commercial incorporation requires direct permission), NOT pip-installable (uv-managed git clone), 6-8 GB VRAM minimum, CPU 'supported but slow' — cannot be embedded in ImageAI; reproduce its concept with matting-model alpha hint + unmix formula + despill instead
onnxruntime: MIT license, official wheels for Windows/macOS/Linux x64 and arm64 — the only heavyweight dependency rembg needs on CPU

feature_ideas.name: YCbCr color-distance keyer
feature_ideas.description: Classic chroma key computing Euclidean distance in the (Cr,Cb) plane with two thresholds: TOL (fully keyed) and softness (ramp to opaque), matching Nim's CHROMA color picker + TOL slider. Luminance-independent, so it survives shaded/uneven AI-generated green fields; pure OpenCV+NumPy, real-time on CPU.

feature_ideas.name: Despill filter suite
feature_ideas.description: Post-key green/blue spill removal offering the standard algorithms (average, double-blue/red average, limit) plus automatic luminance restoration by adding back the desaturated despill difference. Prevents the green fringe that otherwise haloes every extracted sprite frame.

feature_ideas.name: Edge choke, feather, and despeckle controls
feature_ideas.description: Three-slider edge group: choke (mask erode), feather (Gaussian blur on alpha), despeckle (morphological open). Handles the anti-aliased mixed pixels AI image/video models produce at character silhouettes and removes stray keyed specks.

feature_ideas.name: Edge color decontamination (unmix)
feature_ideas.description: CorridorKey-style unmixing on semi-transparent edge pixels: F=(C-(1-a)K)/a against the sampled key color, recovering true foreground color in hair/motion-blur edges instead of gray-green fringe. Cheap NumPy math layered on any keyer or matting output.

feature_ideas.name: AI background removal (rembg)
feature_ideas.description: One-click 'Remove background' with a model dropdown (u2netp 4 MB fast, isnet-anime for cel/sprite characters, isnet-general-use, birefnet-general-lite; size shown per model) running on CPU via onnxruntime. Works when the source has no green screen at all — the 'Corridor Key' toggle position in the Nim UI.

feature_ideas.name: Alpha-matting edge refinement
feature_ideas.description: Optional rembg alpha_matting pass (foreground_threshold=240, background_threshold=10, erode_size=10) that converts a hard segmentation mask into a soft matte for hair and thin limbs. Exposed as a single 'Refine edges' checkbox with the three advanced numbers behind a disclosure.

feature_ideas.name: Every-Nth-frame extractor
feature_ideas.description: Nim's 'FRAMES: Every 8' control: -vf select='not(mod(n,N))' -fps_mode vfr through the existing ffmpeg_utils layer, writing numbered PNGs. Fast because ffmpeg skips undecoded frames; N slider 1-30 with a computed 'yields ~X frames at Y fps' readout.

feature_ideas.name: Target-FPS frame resampling
feature_ideas.description: Alternate extraction mode using -vf fps=12 so users think in output framerate instead of frame stride — the natural unit for game animation (8/10/12/24 fps presets). Duplicates/drops frames to a constant rate, giving even temporal spacing regardless of source fps.

feature_ideas.name: Union-bbox auto-crop + uniform canvas re-pad
feature_ideas.description: Crops all frames of an action to the union of their alpha bounding boxes, then re-pads to one uniform canvas with a selectable anchor (bottom-center default so feet stay planted). This is the step that turns loose keyed frames into consistent, engine-ready sprite cells.
feature_ideas.depends_on: opencv-python or PIL; alpha channel from keyer/rembg

feature_ideas.name: Sub-pixel frame de-jitter
feature_ideas.description: Aligns jittery AI-generated frames using skimage phase_cross_correlation (upsample_factor=10, run on alpha masks so background drift can't bias it), with alpha-centroid alignment as the fast fallback. Removes the wobble that makes video-derived sprite loops look unstable.

feature_ideas.name: Background-drift suppression
feature_ideas.description: For sequences where the AI slowly mutates the 'solid' background: estimate the static background by median-stacking frames, then key each frame against the per-pixel estimate instead of one global color. Rescues clips a fixed-color key would fail on.

feature_ideas.name: ffmpeg-native key preview
feature_ideas.description: Instant whole-clip preview using ffmpeg's built-in chromakey (color/similarity/blend) + despill filters before any per-frame Python processing — one subprocess renders a keyed preview video for scrubbing. Maps 1:1 to the final per-frame pipeline parameters.

feature_ideas.name: Click-to-segment touch-up (MobileSAM)
feature_ideas.description: Interactive fix for frames the automatic key got wrong: click points or drag a box and MobileSAM (27 MB encoder, CPU-interactive) adds/removes regions from the alpha mask via rembg's sam session. The escape hatch that keeps users out of an external editor.

feature_ideas.name: Chroma-ready prompt injection
feature_ideas.description: When the sprite pipeline is active, auto-append background directives to generation prompts ('solid chroma green background #00FF00, flat lighting, no shadows on background, no camera movement, seamless loop') and record the key color in the frame's JSON sidecar so the keyer auto-picks it.
feature_ideas.depends_on: existing prompt pipeline + metadata sidecar convention

feature_ideas.name: Scene-change and duplicate-frame culling
feature_ideas.description: Optional extraction filters: drop near-duplicate frames (ffmpeg mpdecimate or perceptual hash) and split on scene cuts via select='gt(scene,0.4)' or PySceneDetect ContentDetector(threshold=27.0), so idle loops don't waste sheet cells on identical frames.

feature_ideas.name: Model manager with size/license gating
feature_ideas.description: Settings-integrated downloader for matting models showing size before download (u2netp 4 MB to birefnet-general 928 MB), storing them under the app's configurable storage root via get_data_paths(), and flagging non-commercial weights (bria-rmbg) so the default stays MIT-clean.

feature_ideas.name: CorridorKey external-tool bridge
feature_ideas.description: Detect a user-installed CorridorKey checkout and offer it as a premium keying backend for green/blue-screen video (two-stage neural unmixer, ~300 MB checkpoints, 6-8 GB VRAM). Cannot be bundled: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 and not pip-installable, so integration is launch-and-import only.

summary:
The sprite pipeline can be built almost entirely on Pillow + opencv-python + one small pure-Python packer, with zero new binary dependencies. Pillow's Image.quantize(colors≤256, method, kmeans, dither) covers palette reduction: Quantize.MEDIANCUT and Quantize.MAXCOVERAGE are highest quality but reject RGBA input (Pillow silently falls back to FASTOCTREE for RGBA — relevant because sprite frames are RGBA after chroma key), and Quantize.LIBIMAGEQUANT is compiled OUT of all official Pillow wheels because libimagequant is GPLv3 (check at runtime with PIL.features.check_feature("libimagequant")). Dither is only Dither.NONE or Dither.FLOYDSTEINBERG. For animated export, Pillow saves GIF (per-frame duration/disposal lists, transparency index, optimize), APNG since 7.1.0 (save_all + append_images, default_image, per-frame disposal 0-2 and blend 0-1), and animated WebP (save_all, lossless flag, quality, method 0-6). GIF transparency has documented traps: disposal=2 + optimize=True can corrupt delta frames (Pillow issue #7787) and palette remapping can invalidate the transparency index (#6260) — the export path needs a tested "transparent GIF" recipe (disposal=2, optimize off or careful palette pinning).

For quantization beyond Pillow, the Wanadev "imagequant" PyPI package (v1.1.5) is the real libimagequant: wheels for Windows/manylinux/musllinux/macOS, CPython 3.10-3.14, clean API (quantize_pil_image with dithering_level 0.0-1.0, max_colors, min/max_quality). License is the trap: the binding is BSD-3-Clause but the bundled libimagequant is GPLv3-or-later (or paid commercial) — ship it only as an optional, runtime-detected extra, never a hard dependency. pyxelate (sedthh, MIT, 1.7k stars) does attractive HOG-based pixel-art conversion with Bayer/Atkinson/Floyd-Steinberg dithering, but is NOT pip-installable — the PyPI name "pyxelate" is a 2026 placeholder squat ("Reserved name placeholder. No functionality") and the real project installs only from git and pins heavy deps (scikit-learn, scikit-image, numba). Recommend reimplementing the useful ideas (integer downscale → quantize → ordered dither) in-house rather than depending on it. scikit-learn KMeans works but is a ~30MB dependency for something Pillow's kmeans refinement parameter already approximates.

Atlas packing: rectpack (Apache-2.0, pure Python, v0.2.2 from 2021-11-24) is the only real option and it's sufficient — MaxRects (MaxRectsBssf/Bl/Baf/Blsf), Skyline (6 variants incl. waste-map), and Guillotine (18 variants), offline/online modes, sort heuristics, rotation flag, rect_list() returning (bin, x, y, w, h, rid). It's unmaintained-but-stable and tiny; vendoring is viable under Apache-2.0. Palette files are mostly trivial to hand-roll: .gpl is plain text (Pillow even ships a PIL.GimpPaletteFile reader), JASC .pal is 3 header lines + "R G B" rows, .act is a fixed 768-byte RGB table (+optional 4-byte count/transparency footer), Lospec .hex is one hex color per line; only Adobe .ase is a real binary format — the MIT "swatch" package (v0.4.0, 2014, read+write) exists but is old enough that hand-rolling or vendoring is equally sensible. Aseprite's exported spritesheet JSON (frames + meta.frameTags/slices) is a simple documented shape — hand-roll the writer; the PyPI/GitHub .ase parsers (py_aseprite, asepriteio, aseprite-reader) target the binary format and are too niche to depend on.

Preview: QMovie plays GIF natively and animated WebP via the qwebp imageformats plugin shipped in PySide6 wheels (community reports stutter on WebP), but APNG is not supported at all — Qt's PNG handler reads only the first frame (third-party QtApng plugin exists but isn't practical for PySide6). The reliable approach is a custom QTimer + QPixmap frame player over the in-memory frame list: exact FPS, frame stepping, ping-pong, onion skin, and no format decode in the loop. For pixel-art zoom, render with nearest-neighbor: QPixmap.scaled(..., Qt.FastTransformation) or leave QPainter.SmoothPixmapTransform unset; QGraphicsPixmapItem.setTransformationMode(Qt.FastTransformation) for graphics-view scenes. GIF optimization: pygifsicle (MIT, v1.1.0) is only a subprocess wrapper requiring the gifsicle system binary — disallowed per constraints; there is no pure-Python equivalent of gifsicle's inter-frame optimization, but Pillow already writes only the changed rect of subsequent frames and optimize=True prunes unused palette entries, which is good enough for sprite-preview GIFs (game engines consume the PNG sheet/atlas, not the GIF).
key_facts: Pillow Image.quantize signature: quantize(colors=256, method=None, kmeans=0, palette=None, dither=Dither.FLOYDSTEINBERG); colors max 256
Quantize.MEDIANCUT and Quantize.MAXCOVERAGE do NOT support RGBA input; Pillow silently uses FASTOCTREE for RGBA — sprite frames with alpha always get FASTOCTREE unless flattened first

Quantize.LIBIMAGEQUANT is excluded from ALL official Pillow wheels (Windows, manylinux, macOS) because libimagequant is GPLv3; detect at runtime via PIL.features.check_feature(feature="libimagequant")
Pillow dither options are only Dither.NONE and Dither.FLOYDSTEINBERG (no ordered/Bayer dithering built in)

Pillow GIF save: duration and disposal accept a single int or a per-frame list/tuple (milliseconds; disposal 0-3); loop=0 means infinite; transparency=palette index; palette= raw bytes up to 768 bytes

Pillow GIF pitfall (issue #7787): disposal=2 combined with optimize=True can produce corrupt delta frames when the background color index is missing from a frame's palette; workaround is optimize=False or non-2 disposal
Pillow GIF pitfall (issue #6260): internal remap_palette during multi-frame save can change/invalidate info["transparency"] index — transparent animated GIFs need an explicit tested recipe

Pillow APNG write support exists since Pillow 7.1.0 (2020-04-01): save PNG with save_all=True + append_images; params default_image (bool), duration, loop (0=infinite), disposal 0-2, blend 0-1; per-frame lists must match total frame count exactly
Pillow animated WebP: save_all + append_images with duration/loop, lossless (bool), quality 0-100 (default 80), method 0-6 (default 4); requires libwebp >= 0.5.0 (official wheels bundle it)

PyPI package 'imagequant' (Wanadev imagequant-python) v1.1.5: real libimagequant bindings; wheels for Windows, manylinux + musllinux, macOS (x86_64/arm64/universal2), CPython 3.10-3.14; API imagequant.quantize_pil_image(img, dithering_level=0.0-1.0, max_colors=1-256, min_quality=0-100, max_quality=0-100)

LICENSE TRAP: the imagequant binding code is BSD-3-Clause but the bundled libimagequant library is GPLv3-or-later (or paid commercial license) — usable only as an optional user-installed extra, never as a hard dependency of a non-GPL app

pyxelate (sedthh/pyxelate, MIT, 1.7k stars) is NOT on PyPI — the PyPI name 'pyxelate' 0.0.1 (2026-07-05) is a placeholder squat with 'No functionality'; real install is pip install git+https://github.com/sedthh/pyxelate.git with heavy pinned deps (scikit-learn, scikit-image, numba)
pyxelate features worth copying in-house: Bayer-ordered, Atkinson, naive and Floyd-Steinberg dithering; palette transfer via sklearn-style fit/transform; built-in retro palettes (PICO-8, Apple II)
rectpack v0.2.2 (2021-11-24), Apache-2.0, pure Python, dev status Alpha, single maintainer (secnot); stable/unmaintained — vendorable

rectpack algorithms: MaxRectsBl/MaxRectsBssf/MaxRectsBaf/MaxRectsBlsf; SkylineBl/SkylineBlWm/SkylineMwf/SkylineMwfl/SkylineMwfWm/SkylineMwflWm; 18 Guillotine variants; newPacker(mode=PackingMode.Offline, pack_algo=..., sort_algo=SORT_AREA, rotation=bool); rect_list() yields (bin, x, y, w, h, rid)

.gpl (GIMP palette) is plain text: 'GIMP Palette' magic line, optional Name:/Columns:, '#' comments, then 'R G B name' rows — Pillow ships a reader (PIL.GimpPaletteFile); hand-rolling a writer is ~10 lines

JASC .pal is trivial text: line1 'JASC-PAL', line2 '0100', line3 color count, then 'R G B' per line; .act is raw binary: 768 bytes of RGB triplets, optional 4-byte footer = 2-byte BE color count + 2-byte BE transparency index; Lospec .hex = one RRGGBB per line

Adobe .ase (Swatch Exchange) is the only nontrivial palette format (big-endian chunked binary, float32 components, RGB/CMYK/LAB/Gray); PyPI 'swatch' v0.4.0 (MIT, 2014) parses AND writes it — old but the format is frozen; vendoring or hand-rolling equally viable

QMovie (Qt6) supports whatever QImageReader plugins provide: GIF animation is built-in; animated WebP works via the qwebp plugin shipped in PySide6 wheels (known stutter reports); frameCount() can return 0 for some formats; no reverse playback

Qt6 has NO APNG support — the built-in PNG handler reads only the first frame; third-party QtApng plugin (jurplel/QtApng) exists for C++ Qt but is impractical for PySide6 — do not plan APNG preview via QMovie, use a custom player
Reliable preview = custom QTimer + QLabel/QGraphicsView player over in-memory QPixmaps: exact FPS control, frame step, ping-pong, onion skin; convert frames once via PIL ImageQt or QImage.fromData

Pixel-crisp zoom: QPixmap.scaled(size, Qt.KeepAspectRatio, Qt.FastTransformation) = nearest-neighbor; in custom paint, do NOT set QPainter.SmoothPixmapTransform (unset = nearest); QGraphicsPixmapItem.setTransformationMode(Qt.FastTransformation)

pygifsicle v1.1.0 (MIT, 2024-07-06) REQUIRES the external gifsicle system binary (apt-get install gifsicle / manual Windows port) — violates the no-system-binary constraint; no pure-Python gifsicle equivalent exists

Pillow's own GIF writer already does inter-frame delta encoding (writes only the changed rectangle of subsequent frames) and optimize=True prunes unused palette colors — acceptable for preview GIFs; engines consume PNG sheets anyway

Aseprite spritesheet JSON (hash or array flavor) is a simple documented shape: frames{filename: {frame:{x,y,w,h}, rotated, trimmed, spriteSourceSize, sourceSize, duration}}, meta{app, version, image, size, scale, frameTags[{name,from,to,direction}], layers, slices} — hand-roll the writer; existing libs (py_aseprite, asepriteio, PyPI aseprite-reader) parse the BINARY .ase format and are niche/low-activity

opencv-python (already acceptable) covers chroma key: cv2.cvtColor to HSV + cv2.inRange with tolerance, cv2.morphologyEx cleanup, plus green-spill suppression on RGB channels — no new dependency needed

feature_ideas.name: Green-screen chroma key with tolerance + despill
feature_ideas.description: Local background removal for extracted frames using OpenCV HSV inRange with a color picker and tolerance slider (mirrors Nim's CHROMA/TOL controls), morphological cleanup, and green-spill suppression. Outputs RGBA frames ready for quantization.

feature_ideas.name: Every-Nth frame extraction from action clips
feature_ideas.description: Pull sprite frames from Veo/Omni-generated clips via the existing ffmpeg layer ("FRAMES: Every 8" style stride, plus start/end trim). No new dependency; feeds the frame list that every downstream stage consumes.

feature_ideas.name: Palette quantization engine (Pillow)
feature_ideas.description: Reduce frames to N<=256 colors with selectable method (MEDIANCUT/MAXCOVERAGE/FASTOCTREE) and Floyd-Steinberg/none dithering. Must flatten or handle RGBA explicitly since MEDIANCUT/MAXCOVERAGE reject alpha and Pillow silently falls back to FASTOCTREE.

feature_ideas.name: Optional libimagequant high-quality mode
feature_ideas.description: Runtime-detected optional extra using the Wanadev imagequant wheels (quantize_pil_image with dithering_level/max_colors/quality band) for pngquant-grade palettes. Must be opt-in and user-installed: bundled libimagequant is GPLv3-or-commercial, so it cannot be a hard dependency.

feature_ideas.name: Fixed-palette mapping + palette file import
feature_ideas.description: Quantize all frames of all actions to one shared palette (Pillow quantize(palette=img)) so the whole sprite set is consistent, with import of .gpl/.pal/.act/.hex (trivial hand-rolled parsers) and .ase (vendor the MIT swatch parser or hand-roll). Includes built-in retro palettes like PICO-8.

feature_ideas.name: In-house pixel-art downscaler with ordered dithering
feature_ideas.description: Integer downscale-to-sprite-size plus Bayer-ordered and Atkinson dithering implemented in numpy (Pillow only offers Floyd-Steinberg). Borrows pyxelate's ideas without depending on it — pyxelate is git-only (its PyPI name is squatted) and drags in scikit-learn/scikit-image/numba.

feature_ideas.name: Grid sprite-sheet assembly
feature_ideas.description: Compose frames into a fixed-cell grid sheet (rows = actions, columns = frames) with configurable cell size, padding, and alignment, exported as RGBA PNG plus a JSON map. Pure Pillow paste operations.

feature_ideas.name: Packed atlas export (MaxRects)
feature_ideas.description: Tightly packed texture atlas via rectpack (MaxRectsBssf default, rotation toggle, power-of-two bin option) with frame trim-to-bbox before packing and per-frame source offsets recorded in the JSON metadata. rectpack is pure Python Apache-2.0; vendor it since upstream is dormant.

feature_ideas.name: Transparent animated GIF export (safe recipe)
feature_ideas.description: Per-action GIF preview export with per-frame duration lists, disposal=2, and a pinned palette that dodges Pillow's documented transparency traps (optimize+disposal=2 corruption #7787, transparency-index remap #6260). Ship as a tested helper, not raw save() calls.

feature_ideas.name: APNG and animated WebP export
feature_ideas.description: Full-color animated previews without GIF's 256-color limit: APNG via Pillow>=7.1.0 (save_all, default_image, disposal/blend) and animated WebP (lossless flag, quality, method). WebP files preview in-app via QMovie; APNG will not (Qt can't read it) — document that.

feature_ideas.name: Aseprite-compatible JSON metadata writer
feature_ideas.description: Hand-rolled writer for Aseprite's spritesheet JSON (frames hash with frame/spriteSourceSize/sourceSize/duration, meta.frameTags per action, direction forward/pingpong) so sheets drop into Godot/Unity/Phaser importers that already speak this dialect. No dependency worth taking — existing PyPI libs target the binary .ase format.

feature_ideas.name: QTimer frame player preview
feature_ideas.description: Custom playback widget (QTimer + cached QPixmaps) as the primary animation preview: exact FPS spinner, frame step, loop/ping-pong, scrub bar. More reliable than QMovie (no APNG in Qt, WebP stutter reports) and works on in-memory frames before any export.

feature_ideas.name: Pixel-grid zoom view
feature_ideas.description: Nearest-neighbor zoom (Qt.FastTransformation / SmoothPixmapTransform off) with optional pixel grid lines and checkerboard alpha background, in a QGraphicsView so pan/zoom is free. Essential for judging quantization and dithering results at sprite scale.

feature_ideas.name: Onion-skin and loop-seam checker
feature_ideas.description: Overlay adjacent frames at reduced opacity in the preview, and a seam meter that diffs last-vs-first frame (numpy MSE) to grade how 'seamless loop' each AI clip really is — directly supports the per-action prompt cards that request seamless loops.

feature_ideas.name: Source normalization for character input
feature_ideas.description: Prepare the input character image: auto-detect backdrop color by border sampling, center on a transparent square canvas of the target aspect (per the existing no-crop/no-distort rule), and report if the image lacks a clean chroma backdrop before sending to video/image models.

feature_ideas.name: Per-action clip generation from prompt cards
feature_ideas.description: Drive the existing Veo/Omni clients with one short prompt card per action (idle, walk, attack...), each rendered against the green-screen source image — the Nim Animate Studio pipeline step. Library-side this is pure reuse of core/video plus the LLM prompt-card generator.

feature_ideas.name: Local AI background removal fallback
feature_ideas.description: For sources without a clean green screen, offer rembg-style local matting (MIT, onnxruntime-based) as an optional install alongside chroma key — mirrors Nim's Corridor-Key-vs-Chroma-Key toggle. Verify wheel weight and model download UX before committing.

feature_ideas.name: Opportunistic gifsicle post-optimization
feature_ideas.description: If a gifsicle binary is already on PATH, offer an optional post-export optimize pass (pygifsicle or direct subprocess); never require it — pygifsicle is only a wrapper around the system binary, which is out-of-bounds as a dependency. Pillow's delta-frame writing is the default.

summary:
Tab architecture: gui/main_window.py builds all tabs in `_init_ui` (main_window.py:667-728). Simple tabs are bare QWidgets initialized by `_init_*_tab` methods; complex tabs are self-contained QWidget subclasses in their own package — `LayoutTab` (gui/layout/layout_tab.py:30, ~20 modules) is constructed eagerly with `config` and added via `self.tabs.addTab(self.tab_layout, "📖 Layout")` (line 712), while the Video tab uses a lazy pattern: a placeholder QWidget is added at startup and `_load_video_tab` (main_window.py:8116) swaps in `VideoProjectTab(config, providers_dict)` (gui/video/video_project_tab.py:1572) on first tab activation. Cross-tab handoff already exists: LayoutTab emits `sendToImageRequested`/`fillAllRequested` signals that MainWindow connects (lines 700-704) and routes through `_on_layout_send_to_image` (6293) / `_maybe_place_image_in_layout` (6331) — the exact template for "Send to Sprite tab". A Sprite tab should be a `gui/sprite/` package with a `SpriteTab(QWidget)`, lazy-loaded like Video.

Providers: OpenAIProvider (providers/openai.py) is capability-table driven (MODEL_CAPS at line 46) and ALREADY exposes gpt-image's `background` parameter — `generate()` forwards `background` in {transparent, opaque, auto} for gpt-image-1.5 (lines 515-518) and {transparent, white, black} for gpt-image-1/mini (547-550), and raises `_UnsupportedParam` at line 244 if transparent is requested on a model whose caps say `supports_transparent_bg: False` — note the table marks gpt-image-2 as NOT supporting transparent bg ("Use gpt-image-1.5 or gpt-image-1 for alpha PNG output"). `edit_image` (821) supports multi-reference lists + alpha-PNG mask inpainting but does NOT forward `background`; adding it there is a ~5-line change gated on the caps table. GoogleProvider sets aspect ratio via `image_config={'aspect_ratio': ...}` / `types.ImageConfig` in both `generate()` (797-870) and `edit_image()` (1832-1877), accepts `reference_image`/`reference_images` kwargs, auto-centers mismatched-aspect references on a transparent canvas (`apply_transparent_canvas_fix`, google.py:70; inline version at 882-960), and has `edit_image_region` (1907) plus a conversational `create_chat_session` (242) for style-consistent multi-edit — ideal for iterative frame-by-frame sprite generation with Nano Banana. Gemini has no transparent-background parameter; a Sprite "background" option maps to: OpenAI native param, Gemini via green-screen prompting + local keying.

Video pipeline: VeoClient (core/video/veo_client.py) takes `VeoGenerationConfig` (line 66) with `image` (start frame → image-to-video), `last_frame` (Veo 3.1 frame interpolation — perfect for seamless loops: pass the same image as start and end), up to 3 `reference_images`, durations locked to 8s (veo-3.1) or 4/6/8s (veo-3.1-fast), aspect 16:9/9:16/1:1, 720p/1080p, fps 24; plus `generate_batch` (1023), `extend_video` (767), `concatenate_clips` (1055).
